flags.detail: The sole author, Dr. Ravi Kumar, is this journal's own Editor in Chief. Under the journal's policy a manuscript submitted by an editorial-board member must be handled by a different editor (for example the Managing Editor or an independent guest editor), with the author excluded from all decisions on it and from access to reviewer identities. Please record who handled the review. The published article should also carry a competing-interests statement disclosing the author's editorial role. The manuscript contains no such statement and none was added (no invented declarations).

Discussion: the paragraph that follows the Punjab and Haryana chart (Figure 18) was headed 'The High Court of Meghalaya shows an uneven pattern ... Backlog fell sharply by 25.17 % at first then dropped each year', but every other number in it (452,548 -> 423,466; -0.59%, -1.26%, -2.15%, -2.57%; -29,082 = -6.43%) is the Punjab and Haryana data. The court name and the '25.17%' clause had been copied from the Meghalaya paragraph. Corrected to 'The High Court of Punjab and Haryana ...' and 'Backlog dropped each year: in the second year it fell by 0.59%, ...'. The original text is recorded in changes. The author should confirm the correction. The phrase 'uneven pattern' was kept although the data show a steady decline every year.

The text shows strong signs of being run through an automated paraphrasing / 'AI-humaniser' tool. Ordinals and adjectives are systematically deleted: 'in the year' appears about 30 times for 'in the second/third/fourth/fifth year'; 'the right to a trial' stands for 'the right to a speedy trial' (6x); 'the right to an public trial' for the Sixth Amendment's 'speedy and public trial'; 'The findings show a picture' for 'a mixed picture'; 'At the time' for 'At the same time'. First-person fillers are inserted ('I notice', 'I see that', 'I think', 'I feel that'). Commas are misplaced ('rise, in pendency'), the Madras figures are spelled out ('two point one four percent', 'fifty-three thousand five hundred forty cases') and 'which's' is used. Where the chart data or legal context made the meaning unambiguous, the words were restored and each edit is recorded in changes. Supplied words that the author should confirm: 'evidentiary safeguards', 'a good job', 'greater judicial capacity', 'large proportional growth', 'nearly six lakh', 'recorded in the study period'. Recommendation: run a similarity / AI-text check and have the author approve the copy-edited text.

Rajasthan: the text says 'The biggest jump happened between Year 1 and Year 2 when the cases increased by 9.39%', but the final-year rise (10.77%, 616,341 -> 682,725) is larger. The final-year rise is also called 'the big rise ... [that] stands out'. Left unchanged for the author to correct.

Calcutta High Court's 10.44% reduction (2,29,563 -> 2,05,591) is the fourth largest of the 10 reductions, but it is missing from the 'High Courts Showing Reduction in Pendency' list, from Table 1, and from the Final research result and Conclusion lists of successful courts. Patna (-3.14%) appears in Table 1 but not in the bullet list. Table 1 is not in descending order (Telangana -2.70% comes before Patna -3.14%). The '15 increased / 10 decreased' count is correct (verified from the chart data). Not changed. The author should add Calcutta and reorder the table.

The study's main data source (year-wise pendency of 25 High Courts, 2021-2025, said to come from the NJDG and Department of Justice) has no reference entry, URL, access date or reference date (for example 'as on 31 December'). The 'Government of India parliamentary answer' reporting 63,63,406 cases pending as of 8 December 2025 is also uncited. That figure differs from the paper's own 2025 total of 63,90,530, which is likely a different snapshot date that is not stated. Add full data-source citations and the reference date of each annual figure.

The Literature Review and International Perspective make many claims with no citation: the Law Commission's 'several reports', 'Several researchers have stressed ...', 'Articles related to vacancies ...', 'Research using data has also found big differences ...', and the US, UK and Australian practice. The reference list has only 8 entries: 7 case citations (two cases listed twice) and 1 Law Commission report, with no scholarly literature. This is thin for a research article. Recommend that the author add the sources relied on.

The manuscript gives no affiliation, e-mail address or ORCID for the author, only 'Dr. Ravi Kumar, Ph.D. Law'. The affiliation used (Head of Department, Indraprastha Law College, Greater Noida) comes from the journal's editorial-board records. No corresponding-author e-mail is printed because none is known. Please supply one for the first-page footnote. The Word file's document properties name the author as 'DR RAVI TYAGI', so please confirm the name to be published.

No declarations: no competing interests (see the conflict_of_interest flag), funding, or data-availability statement. Received/accepted dates are not stated. Ethics approval is not needed (the study uses only published secondary data on court pendency).

References 3 and 6 (Abdul Rehman Antulay v. R.S. Nayak) and 4 and 7 (P. Ramachandra Rao v. State of Karnataka) cite the same judgments. 3 and 4 add AIR citations, so they are not exact duplicates and all were kept. Recommend merging and renumbering (3->3, 6->3, 4->4, 7->4). Hussainara Khatoon is first discussed without a citation number. It is dated (1979) in the text and reported as (1980) 1 SCC 81 in reference 5. This is consistent (decision year vs report year) but could be harmonised. All 8 references are cited in the text, and every in-text number has an entry.

Small rounding differences between the text and percentages recomputed from the chart data (left unchanged): Allahabad 2024 6.84% (computed 6.85%); Bombay overall 12.41% (12.42%); Delhi 2022 3.94% (3.95%); Gujarat 2023 3.63% (3.62%) and overall 13.52% (13.51%); Chhattisgarh 2024 6.50% (6.51%); Jharkhand 2024 13.27% (13.28%); Manipur 2023 9.62% (9.61%); Rajasthan overall 25.82% (25.81%); Uttarakhand 2025 7.28% (7.29%); Patna 2022 6.13% (6.12%). All other figures (absolute changes, totals, overall percentages, 25-court total = sum of courts) match exactly.

Major Findings, Allahabad: the source sentence 'That is an increase of cases or 18.93 percent' is missing the absolute increase. 'cases or' was removed. From the paper's own figures the increase is 1,94,053 cases (12,18,984 - 10,24,931). The author may add it.

Methodology says the year-to-year % change is computed 'by taking the ratio of the number of cases pending in the current year to the previous year, and multiplying it by 100'. That formula gives an index (e.g. 100.95), not a % change. The figures actually reported are correct percentage changes, ((current - previous) / previous) x 100. Recommend that the author correct the description.

H₀-H₄ are stated but never formally tested or explicitly accepted or rejected. There are no statistical tests, only descriptive percentages. The section called 'Discussion' is really the court-by-court presentation of results and comes before 'Results'.
